questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem:
Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(-1,0),(1,0)$ and $(0,1),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+3xy\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/0dfe132146c4095954d6b628b055317c975fed6ec429b9ad48b68f4015d6c033.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)=3xy.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=3y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+xy\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(3y-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}y\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=y.$

questions.problem:
Consider the quadrilateral $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0),(1,0),(1,1)$ and $(0,2),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\,dx+2xy{e}^{xy}\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/b7fad52bdf54c0870ad4c4939a314f5657e390b589faf76e60a8d8ef5d926039.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{2}{e}^{xy}$ and $Q(x,y)=2xy{e}^{xy}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=(2y+x{y}^{2}){e}^{xy},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=(2y+2x{y}^{2}){e}^{xy}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\,dx+2xy{e}^{xy}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[(2y+2x{y}^{2}){e}^{xy}-(2y+x{y}^{2}){e}^{xy}]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y+2x{y}^{2}-2y-x{y}^{2}){e}^{xy}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x{y}^{2}{e}^{xy}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}{e}^{xy}.$

$$
{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+{x}^{2}\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/aa60dd35a920d166f7cc3238a366bde93bd2c33e1b39b0a38313ab46a8de2d8b.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+{x}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x-2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2(x-y)\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=2(x-y).$

questions.problem:
Consider the path $C,$ in the plane, as the boundary of the region enclosed by the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=1,$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2y\,dx+{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise. Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/c44b320dd7ba2824ae0024a3d77d0c6cd6e06fa5889e23879f3d6f464c3a80df.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2y$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}{e}^{x}\operatorname{cos}⁡2y\,dx+{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y-(-2{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y)]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y+2{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)=3{e}^{x}\operatorname{sin}⁡2y.$

questions.problem:
Consider the rectangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0),(2,0),(2,1)$ and $(0,1),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
{∮}_{C}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dy={∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,\text{d}A.
$$

Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/8d57fb7f6b8e2e822a11f11a0267994c449c37b43df167a8d48ab8036854b8dd.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡y-{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(y\operatorname{sin}⁡y-{x}^{2}y)\,dx+(x\operatorname{sin}⁡y+xy\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}[\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡y-(\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡y-{x}^{2})]\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y+y\operatorname{cos}⁡y-\operatorname{sin}⁡y-y\operatorname{cos}⁡y+{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{2}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y)={x}^{2}.$

questions.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral as a Repeated Integral Using Green's Theorem
questions.problem: Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0),(0,-1)$ and $(1,0),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ Express ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$  where $F(x,y)=⟨x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,x\operatorname{sin}⁡y⟩,$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/6d4f13abad5cc193dccedee3114fbd9cbd9fb8e6b5b3ddb0d07f0ed2ed51f4ff.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y$ and $Q(x,y)=x\operatorname{sin}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-x\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le y+1,\,-1\le y\le 0}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{y+1}(1+x)\operatorname{sin}⁡y\text{ }dx\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/e48034aed1f41cf1f9b30c057186879233fe05cd2ba720dcee436398a732b6ce.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}y\operatorname{cos}⁡x\,dx+(x-{e}^{-{y}^{2}})\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ and $Q(x,y)=x-{e}^{-{y}^{2}}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=1.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 1,\,0\le y\le \sqrt{1-{x}^{2}}}

$$

questions.problem: Consider the closed curve $C,$ which is the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $y={x}^{2}$ and $y=x+2.$ Express ${∮}_{C}F\cdot dr,$  where $F(x,y)=⟨\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+x)-{y}^{2},{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}⟩,$ as a repeated integral.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/e32b8e7d6ce80d7cedad928f9a2f7acc3c3d7f06add7909e856db27d154068d6.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+x)-{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡(2+x)-{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-1\le x\le 2,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le x+2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(\operatorname{ln}⁡(1+x)-{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x+2y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{x+2}2(x+y)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}(2y-x)\,dx+(5x-y)\,dy,$ where $C$ is the boundary of the region enclosed by the curves $y=x$ and $y={x}^{2}-x.$
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/e788bbcbda4cc715c6989b7de9d08d60e3b0d178eeb9432a342a4c86c4c01b86.png)

We have that $P(x,y)=2y-x$ and $Q(x,y)=5x-y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =5.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\,{x}^{2}-x\le y\le x}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(2y-x)\,dx+(5x-y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(5-2)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3\,\text{d}A \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}-x}^{x}\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}[y]_{{x}^{2}-x}^{x}\,dx \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2}(2x-{x}^{2})\,dx \\  & =3{[{x}^{2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =3(4-\frac{8}{3}) \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 3,\,\frac{{x}^{2}}{3}\le y\le \sqrt{3x}}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}2xy\,dx+{y}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(0-2x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{{x}^{2}/3}^{\sqrt{3x}}(-2x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2x)[y]_{{x}^{2}/3}^{\sqrt{3x}}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(-2x)(\sqrt{3x}-\frac{{x}^{2}}{3})dx \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{3}(\sqrt{3}{x}^{3/2}-\frac{{x}^{3}}{3})dx \\  & =-2{[\frac{2{x}^{2}\sqrt{3x}}{5}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{12}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =-2(\frac{2(3)^{2}\sqrt{3(3)}}{5}-\frac{(3)^{4}}{12}) \\  & =-2(\frac{54}{5}-\frac{27}{4}) \\  & =-\frac{81}{10}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate ${∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy,$ where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(2,2)$ and $(-2,2),$ traversed counterclockwise.
questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/7ca4b6fe3a5a16c4004c75b0e4524cc3b42550cb2413d5b8e1c21a1d53cee902.png)

We have that $P(x,y)={e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y$ and $Q(x,y)={e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-2{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2{y}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):-y\le x\le y,\,0\le y\le 2}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({e}^{x}-2{x}^{2}y)\,dx+({e}^{y}+2x{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2{y}^{2}+2{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-y}^{y}(2{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}2{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}+x{y}^{2}]}_{-y}^{y}\,dy \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}(\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+{y}^{3}+\frac{{y}^{3}}{3}+{y}^{3})dy \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{8{y}^{3}}{3}\,dy \\  & =\frac{16}{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & =\frac{4}{3}{[{y}^{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\cdot {2}^{4} \\  & =\frac{64}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/73bf9b973e50c540a873f4f1a44d936474e4c49d7041a330902508a840645009.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}({x}^{3}+2{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)={x}^{3}+2{y}^{2}$ and $Q(x,y)={x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):y\le x\le 2-y,\,0\le y\le 1}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}({x}^{3}+2{y}^{2})\,dx+({x}^{2}+\operatorname{ln}⁡y)\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x-4y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{y}^{2-y}(2x-4y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[{x}^{2}-4xy]}_{y}^{2-y}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[(2-y)^{2}-4(2-y)y-{y}^{2}+4{y}^{2}]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(8{y}^{2}-12y+4)\,dy \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{1}(2{y}^{2}-3y+1)\,dy \\  & =4{[\frac{2{y}^{3}}{3}-\frac{3{y}^{2}}{2}+y]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =4[\frac{2}{3}-\frac{3}{2}+1] \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$

$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/5f34ac74599937e0ae181126ff9a3da5b29dfe213614a1f23ca10c7062f22f7d.png)

First, notice that we can rewrite our integral as follows:

$$
{∮}_{C}F\cdot dr={∮}_{C}(3xy-1)\,dx+(3{x}^{2}+{e}^{y})\,dy
$$

We have that $P(x,y)=3xy-1$ and $Q(x,y)=3{x}^{2}+{e}^{y}.$ Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3x,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =6x.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D={(x,y):0\le x\le 2,\,{x}^{2}\le y\le 2x}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}(3xy-1)\,dx+(3{x}^{2}+{e}^{y})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(6x-3x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}3x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{{x}^{2}}^{2x}3x\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3x[y]_{{x}^{2}}^{2x}\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}3x(2x-{x}^{2})\,dx \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(6{x}^{2}-3{x}^{3})\,dx \\  & ={[2{x}^{3}-\frac{3{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =2(2)^{3}-\frac{3(2)^{4}}{4} \\  & =16-12 \\  & =4.\end{aligned}

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Expressing a Line Integral as a Double Integral Using Green's Theorem
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0), (1,0)$ and $(0,2),$ and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ According to Green's theorem, 

$$
\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}\cos{y}\,\mathrm{d}x+x\sin{y}\,\mathrm{d}y}= \iint\limits_D f(x,y) \,\textrm d A,
$$

where $C$ is traversed counterclockwise. Calculate the function $f(x,y).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/a78a98750e3203760d27daaebd42852198538935e2c3777a0b8a8c85d1bb0901.png)

We have that $P(x,y)= \cos{y}$ and $Q(x,y)= x\sin{y}.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-\operatorname{sin}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,dx+x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\operatorname{sin}⁡y-(-\operatorname{sin}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, $f(x,y) = 2\sin{y}.$

canonical_examples.problem: Consider the triangle $C$ in the plane with vertices $(0,0), (1,1)$ and $(-1,1),$ traversed counterclockwise, and the region $D$ bounded by $C.$ Express $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C}x\sin{y}\,\mathrm{d}x+ (x^2\cos{y}-y^2)\,\mathrm{d}y}$ as a repeated integral.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\,\textrm d A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/2fa3c84359cec5f5e0750552e5a4b24b20b8dbc3d65b909aea908e1505cfb5e3.png)

We have that $P(x,y)= x\sin{y}$ and $Q(x,y)= x^2\cos{y}-y^2.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=x\operatorname{cos}⁡y,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type II region as follows:

$$
D = \{(x,y) :  -y\leq x\leq y,\, 0\leq y \leq 1\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,dx+({x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡y-{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2x\operatorname{cos}⁡y-x\operatorname{cos}⁡y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-y}^{y}x\operatorname{cos}⁡y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.problem: Use Green's theorem to evaluate $\displaystyle{\oint\limits_{C} 4x^2y \, \mathrm{d}x+ 2y^2\,\mathrm{d}y},$ where $C$ is the boundary of the triangle with vertices at $(0,0),$ $(1,2)$ and $(0,2),$ traversed counterclockwise.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D$, then Green's theorem states that

$$
\oint\limits_{C} P\,\mathrm{d}x + Q\,\mathrm{d}y 
= \iint\limits_D \left(\frac{\partial Q}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial P}{\partial y}\right)\textrm d A.
$$

The region $D$ and the curve $C$ for this case are shown below.

 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061381/assets/a87f696b1eb42588ab69800b72d821bf47b35676fc19dcd4fe2927bbf36ba3f8.png)

We have that $P(x,y)= 4x^2y$ and $Q(x,y)= 2y^2.$ So,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂P}{∂y}=4{x}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We can express the region $D$ as a type I region as follows:

$$
D = \left\{(x,y) : 0 \leq x \leq 1,\, 2x \leq y \leq 2 \right\}
$$

Therefore, applying Green's Theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}4{x}^{2}y\,dx+2{y}^{2}\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(0-4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{2x}^{2}(-4{x}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}[y]_{2x}^{2}\,dx \\  & =-4{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(2-2x)\,dx \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}(1-x)\,dx \\  & =-8{\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}\,dx \\  & =-8{[\frac{{x}^{3}}{3}-\frac{{x}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-8(\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{4}) \\  & =-8\cdot \frac{1}{12} \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$
